title: Rejecting extremism
hook: scholars have condemned terrorism as against Islam, as in the Open Letter to al-Baghdadi

segments.voice: Yesterday: Islamic finance, trade permitted, riba forbidden, and an honest argument about the difference. Your line was finance without interest. Today, a harder question, and a new week.

The letter is addressed to one man, by name: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, who had declared himself caliph of the group called ISIS, and to the fighters who followed him. Not to the world, not to the press. It's written in Arabic, in the language of the law he claimed to be applying, and signed by Muslim scholars and leaders from many countries. Its message, point after point, is a single word: no.
screen: `ADDRESSED TO ONE MAN.` → `WRITTEN IN HIS OWN TERMS.` → `ONE WORD: NO.`

segments.voice: The Open Letter to al-Baghdadi doesn't shout. It argues, verse by verse, like a teacher marking an exam. Issuing religious rulings without the learning they require is forbidden. Killing the innocent is forbidden. Killing emissaries is forbidden, and so killing journalists and aid workers is too. Torture is forbidden. Declaring other Muslims to be unbelievers, when they haven't declared it themselves, is forbidden. And fighting in Islam has rules, a right cause and a right conduct, and isn't permitted without them. Behind those points sit texts anyone can read. In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall: "Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors." And in Sunan an-Nasa'i the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, warns against going to extremes in religion, saying, in paraphrase, that people before you were destroyed by it. The Arabic word is ghuluw: overshooting, going past the mark. Read beside the letter, the hadith names the charge. Not too much religion. Excess that leaves religion behind. And the letter is one statement among several. Scholars in different countries have issued their own fatwas and declarations against terrorism, in mosques and in print, public for anyone to read. They say, in their own words, what today's line says in three.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT, POINT BY POINT.` · `BEGIN NOT HOSTILITIES.` · `GHULUW: GOING PAST THE MARK.` · `SIGNED, DATED, AND PUBLIC.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a headline that used a faith's name for an act of violence; you don't have to replay the images, just notice how the story usually ends there. Now add the part that rarely gets told: somewhere, a scholar sat down and wrote an answer, with the line from al-Baqarah behind it, begin not hostilities. If you pray, pray for those harmed in that faith's name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.
Rejecting extremism. Scholars answering violence done in Islam's name with the Qur'an and hadith, as in the Open Letter to al-Baghdadi. Today's word.
Your line: scholars said no. Point by point, in their own terms and texts. Until tomorrow.
